useCases.title: "Continue Where You Left Off" Browse Recall
useCases.oneLiner: Bring back recently viewed products and categories on return visits and via a follow-up email.
useCases.journey: A visitor browses trail running shoes for 6 minutes, views 3 product pages, then leaves without buying. The CDP captures the viewed SKUs and category signal in real time. On their next visit within 7 days, the homepage swaps its generic hero for a "Continue browsing" module showing those exact products plus two complementary items. If they don't return within 24 hours, a single triggered email repeats the same logic.
useCases.exampleBefore: Generic homepage hero: "New Season Arrivals"
useCases.exampleAfter: "Still thinking about the Velocity Trail 30? Runners who viewed this also loved these trail-ready picks."

useCases.title: Purchase-History-Driven Homepage Hero
useCases.oneLiner: Swap the homepage hero and featured collection based on a customer's past category and sport affinity.
useCases.personalizationTactic: Dynamic hero / module swapping by segment
useCases.journey: A customer who bought trail running shoes three months ago logs back in. Instead of the same generic seasonal banner every visitor sees, the homepage hero and the first product carousel are swapped for new trail-shoe arrivals and matching trail apparel, using a simple rule built on their purchase category history.
useCases.exampleBefore: Homepage hero: "Shop the New Collection" (identical for every visitor)
useCases.exampleAfter: "Back for more trails? Here's what just landed in Trail Running."
toolsNeeded: Web/app personalization engine or CMS with segment rules

useCases.title: Loyalty-Tier Aware Perks Bar
useCases.oneLiner: Show a persistent, tier-specific perks message instead of the same static banner for everyone.
useCases.journey: A Gold-tier loyalty member sees a sticky top bar reading "You're 200 points from Platinum — free shipping is already unlocked." A non-member browsing the same page instead sees "Join Insider Rewards and get 10% off your first order." Both use the exact same UI slot; only the CDP-driven content differs.
useCases.exampleBefore: Static banner: "Free shipping over €75" for all visitors
useCases.exampleAfter: "200 points to Platinum" (member) vs. "Join free, get 10% off" (guest)

useCases.title: Weather & Location-Triggered Recommendations
useCases.oneLiner: Trigger a push notification and matching landing page when local weather or season shifts align with a customer's habits.
cdpDataUsed: Local weather feed matched to profile
useCases.journey: Rain is forecast tomorrow in a customer's region, and their profile shows a history of road running plus no waterproof shoe in their purchase history. A push notification fires: "Rain expected tomorrow — here's a shoe that handles it." Tapping it opens an app landing page pre-filtered to GORE-TEX products in their size and gender.
useCases.exampleBefore: Generic push: "20% off this weekend" sent to the entire app user base
useCases.exampleAfter: "Rain tomorrow in Amsterdam — the Velocity Storm GTX keeps you dry" sent only to relevant road runners in that postcode

useCases.title: Product Lifecycle Replenishment Series
useCases.oneLiner: Remind customers to replace a product right when it's statistically due, not on an arbitrary calendar date.
cdpDataUsed: Category average lifespan (e.g. running shoe ≈ 500-800km or 6 months)
Stated weekly mileage or activity level
useCases.journey: A customer bought running shoes 5 months ago and told the brand (via app or loyalty quiz) that they run 30km/week. The CDP calculates their shoes are approaching typical end-of-life around month 5.5. A timed email arrives: "Your Velocity Trail 30s have probably covered ~450km — here's when runners like you usually replace them," with a tailored replacement SKU and a trade-in/recycle CTA.
useCases.exampleBefore: No reminder — customer discovers worn-out shoes mid-run and buys a competitor's product
useCases.exampleAfter: "Time for fresh legs? Your shoes are due for retirement around now."

useCases.title: Personalized Search & Category Sort Order
useCases.oneLiner: Re-rank search and category results so the most relevant products for this specific shopper appear first.
useCases.personalizationTactic: Personalized ranking / re-ranking of search & PLP results
useCases.journey: A customer who has previously bought women's trail shoes in size 39 searches "running shoes." Instead of a one-size-fits-all relevance sort, results are re-ranked so women's trail options in size 39 surface first — without hiding the rest of the catalog, so discovery isn't lost.
useCases.exampleBefore: Search "running shoes" returns the same generic best-seller order for every visitor
useCases.exampleAfter: Same search returns her usual size, gender, and terrain preference first, best-sellers below
toolsNeeded: CDP feeding a search/merchandising platform (e.g. Algolia, Coveo) with a personalization API

useCases.title: Value-Tiered Cart Recovery
useCases.oneLiner: Recover abandoned carts with an incentive matched to the customer's value and discount sensitivity, not a blanket coupon.
useCases.personalizationTactic: Segmented incentive logic in a triggered journey
useCases.journey: A high-CLV customer who has never redeemed a discount code abandons a cart. Their recovery email leads with free shipping and a styling tip — no discount, protecting margin. A first-time, price-sensitive visitor who abandons the same cart instead receives a 10%-off code, because the CDP's segment data shows this nudge is what typically converts them.
useCases.exampleBefore: Everyone who abandons a cart gets the same 15% discount code, including customers who would have paid full price
useCases.exampleAfter: High-value customers get a no-discount nudge; price-sensitive segments get a targeted incentive

useCases.title: New vs. Returning Visitor Onsite Messaging
useCases.oneLiner: Stop offering first-purchase discounts to loyal customers — differentiate the welcome message by identity.
useCases.journey: A first-time anonymous visitor lands on the site and sees "New here? Get 15% off your first pair." A recognized returning customer who bought last month instead sees "Welcome back, Alex — here's what's new in Running," with no discount offered, preserving margin on a customer who didn't need one to convert.
useCases.exampleBefore: Every visitor, new or loyal, sees the same first-purchase discount banner
useCases.exampleAfter: New visitors see an acquisition offer; recognized customers see relevant new arrivals instead

useCases.title: Zero-Party Onboarding Quiz → Personalized App Feed
useCases.oneLiner: Ask 3-4 quick questions at sign-up so the app can personalize from day one, before any behavioral data exists.
cdpDataUsed: Zero-party data: running goal, terrain preference, injury history, foot strike
Enriched later with behavioral/app usage data
useCases.journey: A new app user completes a 4-question quiz: "What's your main goal — road, trail, or race training?" The CDP stores the answers as zero-party data immediately, and the app's home feed, training content, and push cadence adapt from the very first session, instead of showing generic content until enough behavioral data accumulates over weeks.
useCases.exampleBefore: New users see a generic "Getting Started" feed identical for everyone, for their first several weeks
useCases.exampleAfter: "You told us you're training for a trail race — here's a 12-week plan and gear picks for it."

useCases.title: Predictive Churn / Win-Back Journey
useCases.oneLiner: Use a predictive lifecycle score to reach out before a good customer fully disengages, not months after.
cdpDataUsed: Engagement decay signals (email opens, app opens, site visits)
useCases.journey: The CDP's lifecycle model flags a previously frequent customer as "at risk": no purchase or engagement in 90 days, versus their usual ~45-day cadence. An automated journey begins with a value-reminder email, followed by a personalized product email based on their past category if they don't respond, then light-touch retargeting. The journey stops automatically the moment the customer shows a reactivation signal.
useCases.exampleBefore: A blanket "We miss you" email sent to the entire inactive list every quarter, regardless of past value or cadence
useCases.exampleAfter: A targeted, staged journey triggered the moment a high-value customer's own normal cadence is broken

secondary: Unsubscribe rate reduction vs. blanket campaigns

useCases.title: Send-Time & Frequency Personalization
useCases.oneLiner: Deliver each email when that individual actually tends to open it, instead of one blast time for everyone.
cdpDataUsed: Historical email open times per customer
useCases.journey: Two customers get the same weekly newsletter. One consistently opens emails around 7am before work; the other almost always opens around 9pm. Instead of a single 10am send time for the whole list, the ESP uses each person's historical open-time pattern (fed by the CDP) to deliver the same email at the moment each is most likely to actually see it.
useCases.exampleBefore: Entire list receives the campaign at 10:00 AM, regardless of individual behavior
useCases.exampleAfter: Same email, delivered at 7:03 AM to morning openers and 9:15 PM to evening openers
toolsNeeded: CDP or ESP with send-time optimization capability

useCases.title: Segment-Aware Subject Lines & Preview Text
useCases.oneLiner: Swap subject line framing by segment (deal-seeker vs. loyalist vs. category fan) instead of one subject line for the whole send.
useCases.personalizationTactic: Dynamic subject line / preview text by segment
useCases.journey: The same new-arrivals campaign goes out to the full list, but the subject line adapts: price-sensitive segments see "20% off new arrivals", loyalty members see "Early access: new arrivals before anyone else", and category-affine customers see a subject naming their specific sport. Same email content, three subject line variants driving the open.
useCases.exampleBefore: "New Arrivals Are Here" sent to 100% of the list, identical subject line
useCases.exampleAfter: "Early access: new arrivals before anyone else" (loyalty) vs. "20% off new arrivals" (deal-seekers)
toolsNeeded: ESP with dynamic subject line blocks

useCases.title: Inactive Subscriber Re-Engagement & Sunset Flow
useCases.oneLiner: Win back fading email subscribers before they go cold, and stop mailing the ones who won't come back.
useCases.journey: A subscriber who used to open every campaign hasn't opened in 60 days. Before they're marked fully inactive, they get a short re-engagement series asking what they'd rather hear about (or offering to reduce frequency). Those who still don't engage after the series are automatically suppressed from regular sends, protecting deliverability for everyone else instead of quietly mailing a growing dead list forever.
useCases.exampleBefore: Dead subscribers keep receiving full-frequency campaigns indefinitely, dragging down open rates and deliverability
useCases.exampleAfter: "We've noticed you haven't opened lately — want fewer, more relevant emails?" before automatic suppression

secondary: Reactivation rate of the sunset series

useCases.title: Gamified Points Progress Nudges
useCases.oneLiner: Turn a static points balance into an active nudge — "you're this close" — shown right when it's motivating.
useCases.journey: A member has 380 of the 400 points needed for a reward, and just added an item to cart that would push them over. At checkout, a small module shows: "This order gets you to your next reward — 20 points away." The nudge only appears when it's actually true and close, not as a generic reminder.
useCases.exampleBefore: Points balance is only visible if the customer digs into their account page
useCases.exampleAfter: "This order unlocks your next reward — only 20 points away!" shown at checkout

useCases.title: Personalized Reward Redemption Suggestions
useCases.oneLiner: Tell members exactly what they can redeem right now, in terms of products they actually want.
useCases.journey: A member has enough points sitting unused for months to redeem for a free pair of socks or a discount — but never has, because they never made the connection. A monthly email shows exactly what their balance can get them right now, framed around products from their preferred category, instead of a generic "don't forget your points!" reminder.
useCases.exampleBefore: "You have 850 points!" with no indication of what that's actually worth
useCases.exampleAfter: "Your 850 points = a free pair of running socks, or €15 off your next pair of Velocity Trail 30s"

useCases.title: Customer-Controlled Frequency & Channel Preference Center
useCases.oneLiner: Let customers set their own contact frequency and topics instead of guessing — and actually honor it.
useCases.journey: Instead of a binary subscribe/unsubscribe link, the footer of every email links to a preference center: how often (weekly / monthly / sale-only), and what topics (new arrivals, promotions, training content). A customer who sets "monthly, promotions only" simply stops receiving the daily general newsletter — before they get frustrated enough to unsubscribe entirely.
useCases.exampleBefore: Only choice is "unsubscribe from everything"
useCases.exampleAfter: "Tell us how often you'd like to hear from us" — frequency and topic controls that are actually respected

useCases.title: Engagement-Based Push Notification Cadence
useCases.oneLiner: Send push less often to people who are tuning it out, and reserve high-frequency pushes for people who actually engage.
useCases.journey: Two users get 4 push notifications a week by default. One taps almost every one; cadence for them can safely increase during a launch week. The other hasn't tapped one in a month — instead of continuing to push (and risking a full opt-out or uninstall), cadence automatically tapers down and shifts to only the highest-relevance moments.
useCases.exampleBefore: Every user gets the same push frequency regardless of whether they engage with it
useCases.exampleAfter: Highly engaged users get more; disengaging users get fewer, more relevant-only pushes
toolsNeeded: Push provider with frequency capping rules

useCases.title: In-App Milestone & Achievement Moments
useCases.oneLiner: Recognize meaningful personal milestones (distance run, order count, membership anniversary) inside the app, not just marketing sends.
useCases.journey: A customer logs their 100th kilometer in the app, or hits their one-year membership anniversary. Instead of that passing unnoticed, the app surfaces a small in-the-moment celebration screen — a badge, a related reward, or just recognition — right when it happens, not in a batch email days later.
useCases.exampleBefore: Milestones pass silently; the app has no idea (or doesn't act on it)
useCases.exampleAfter: "100km logged! Here's a small thank-you." surfaced the moment the milestone is hit

useCases.title: Cross-Device Recently Viewed Sync
useCases.oneLiner: Carry "recently viewed" and cart context between app and web instead of resetting every time the customer switches device.
useCases.journey: A customer browses running shoes on the app during their commute, then opens the website on their laptop that evening. Instead of starting from zero, the site recognizes them (once logged in or identity-resolved) and shows "Continue where you left off" with the same products and cart contents — the two channels behave like one brand instead of two disconnected ones.
useCases.exampleBefore: Cart and browsing history reset completely when switching from app to web
useCases.exampleAfter: Cart and recently-viewed items carry over seamlessly between app and web
toolsNeeded: Unified cart/session API shared by web and app

useCases.title: One Consistent Offer Across Channels
useCases.oneLiner: Make sure a customer sees the same active offer everywhere, instead of a different (or conflicting) one per channel.
useCases.journey: A customer is emailed a 15%-off code. Later that day they open the app, where a completely different (and lower-value) generic promo is showing, creating confusion about what's actually valid. Centralizing "what offer is this customer currently eligible for" in the CDP and reading from that single source everywhere means the app, site, and email all show the same, current offer.
useCases.exampleBefore: Email says 15% off; app banner shows a different, unrelated 10% off promo the same day
useCases.exampleAfter: The same active 15% offer is reflected consistently in email, app, and onsite messaging

secondary: Customer trust/satisfaction proxy (support contacts about offers)

toolsNeeded: CDP as single source of truth for active offers
Shared promo API consumed by all channels

useCases.title: Guided Selling / Shop-by-Activity Quiz
useCases.oneLiner: Help overwhelmed shoppers narrow hundreds of SKUs down to 3-4 relevant picks through a short guided quiz.
useCases.journey: A first-time visitor lands on a category page with 200+ shoe options and doesn't know where to start. A "Find your shoe" guided quiz (3 questions: activity, terrain, arch support need) narrows it to 3 recommended products immediately — and those answers are stored in the CDP as zero-party data for every future visit and email.
useCases.exampleBefore: A 200-product grid with generic filters (size, color, price) and no guidance
useCases.exampleAfter: "Answer 3 quick questions and we'll find your shoe" → 3 tailored recommendations

useCases.title: Personalized Size & Fit Recommendation
useCases.oneLiner: Recommend the right size using a customer's own purchase and return history, not a generic size chart.
useCases.journey: A returning customer previously bought a size 42 in one model and exchanged it for a 42.5 because it ran small. On a new product page, instead of a generic size chart, they see "Based on your past orders, we recommend size 42.5 in this model" — reducing the guesswork that normally drives size-related returns.
useCases.exampleBefore: Generic size chart identical for every visitor, regardless of purchase/return history
useCases.exampleAfter: "We recommend size 42.5 for you in this style, based on your past orders"

useCases.title: Post-Purchase Care & Styling Content
useCases.oneLiner: Follow up after a purchase with content relevant to that exact product, not silence until the next promotional blast.
useCases.journey: A customer buys their first pair of trail running shoes. A week later — once they've likely worn them — they get a short, useful email: care tips for trail shoes, and how to break them in properly, with a soft nudge toward matching trail apparel. It's helpful first, promotional second, and it's the first message they get after checkout instead of nothing until the next sale email.
useCases.exampleBefore: No communication between the order confirmation and the next generic marketing email
useCases.exampleAfter: "5 tips for breaking in your new trail shoes" one week after delivery, with related product ideas

useCases.title: Lifecycle-Timed Review Requests
useCases.oneLiner: Ask for a review when the customer has actually used the product long enough to have an opinion — not the day after delivery.
useCases.journey: Instead of a review request 2 days after delivery (before the product has even been used), the email is timed to typical usage patterns — for running shoes, that might be 10-14 days, enough for a few runs. Customers who've already left several reviews in the past might get asked sooner, since they're known to respond quickly.
useCases.exampleBefore: "Rate your purchase!" sent 2 days after delivery, before the product has been used
useCases.exampleAfter: Review request timed to when the customer has plausibly used the product enough to have a real opinion

useCases.title: Purchase-Based Ad Suppression via CDP Audience Sync
useCases.oneLiner: Stop paying to retarget customers with a product they already bought — sync real purchase data straight to ad platforms.
useCases.journey: A customer buys a pair of running shoes on Monday. Under the old setup, retargeting ads for that exact shoe keep following them around for the next two weeks anyway, because the ad platform doesn't know they already bought it. Syncing purchase events from the CDP to the ad platform's audience in near-real-time suppresses that specific product from their retargeting — and can redirect the budget toward a complementary category instead.
useCases.exampleBefore: Retargeting ads keep showing a product for weeks after the customer already bought it
useCases.exampleAfter: Purchased products are suppressed from retargeting within hours; budget shifts to complementary categories

kpis.primary: Retargeting spend efficiency (cost per incremental conversion)

toolsNeeded: Ad platform integration (Meta/Google Customer Match or equivalent)

useCases.title: In-Content Progressive Profiling Micro-Surveys
useCases.oneLiner: Collect a little zero-party data at a time through short, contextual one-question prompts instead of one long form nobody finishes.
useCases.journey: Instead of a 15-field signup form that most people abandon, the site asks one short, relevant question at a time, in context — e.g. after someone views three trail-running product pages, a small non-blocking prompt asks "What's your main terrain — road, trail, or track?" Answering instantly sharpens their profile; skipping costs nothing. Over a few sessions, a rich profile builds up with almost no friction at any single moment.
useCases.exampleBefore: One long signup form up front; most fields left blank or the form abandoned entirely
useCases.exampleAfter: "Quick one — what's your main terrain?" asked in context, one question at a time, over multiple visits

useCases.title: Per-Provider Email Cadence and Content Personalization for HCPs
useCases.oneLiner: Learn each prescriber's preferred content, timing, frequency and format to cut email opt-outs.
useCases.personalizationTactic: Tailor send frequency, content, and timing per provider
cdpDataUsed: Email engagement history (opens, clicks, opt-outs) across brands
Preferred send time and channel signals
useCases.journey: The CDP unifies several years of email engagement data for healthcare providers across all brands, then a model scores each provider on preferred content, send times, frequency, and format. Brands are consolidated into one per-provider engagement plan. Providers who opened or clicked a topic receive more of it, while low-interest or over-contacted brands are throttled or suppressed. Plans refresh on a regular cadence, and the same preferences are shared with web and other channels so messaging stays consistent.
useCases.exampleBefore: A provider receives dozens of promotional emails a month from many brands, including ones unrelated to their practice, and opts out of all email.
useCases.exampleAfter: The provider gets two relevant emails a month on their preferred topic, sent on Tuesday mornings in a short format, and opt-outs fall by half.

kpis.primary: Email opt-out rate per provider segment

toolsNeeded: CDP with unified profile and identity resolution
Machine learning propensity and send-time model
Email service provider with frequency caps

source.title: Email marketing personalization case study | Deloitte US

useCases.title: Personalized Patient Website and Education Journey
useCases.oneLiner: Tailor patient website content, care prompts, and education by known condition and encounter data.
useCases.personalizationTactic: Show condition-specific content and care prompts based on encounters
useCases.journey: A patient visits the provider website or app. The CDP unifies known patient attributes (condition flags, recent encounter type, preferred location, declared interests) with anonymous browsing and search signals. Homepage and landing modules swap in relevant content: a find-a-PCP prompt for patients without a primary care provider, nearby specialists and closest open office hours, and education on the condition tied to a recent urgent care visit or search. The same segment drives matching follow-up emails with condition tips and appointment reminders, so the patient sees one consistent story across channels. Content must follow consent and health-privacy rules, so sensitive attributes are used only with explicit opt-in and never exposed in visible messaging.
useCases.exampleBefore: A patient who had a recent urgent care visit for a sinus infection lands on the homepage and sees the same generic service banners as every other visitor, then receives a generic newsletter a week later.
useCases.exampleAfter: The same patient sees a sinus-care guide, the closest open clinic with hours, and a book-appointment prompt on the homepage, followed by a matching email with self-care tips and a reminder for a follow-up visit.

kpis.primary: Appointment booking conversion rate from personalized web and email journeys
secondary: Patient portal and app engagement rate
Share of patients with a primary care provider linked
Email click-through rate on education content
Content engagement depth on condition pages

toolsNeeded: EHR or encounter data feed with consent management

source.title: Personalization in Healthcare: Patient Experience Use Cases - Mphasis Silverline

useCases.title: Personalized Patient Appointment and Care-Reminder Emails
useCases.oneLiner: Tailor patient reminder and care-program emails by service line, preferences, and declared needs.
useCases.personalizationTactic: Vary reminder content and send timing by service line and preference
cdpDataUsed: Declared communication preferences and channel opt-ins
Web portal engagement and content views
useCases.journey: A patient books an appointment or enrolls in a care program on the provider's website. The CDP stores the service line, appointment date, and communication preferences. Before each visit, the patient receives a tailored reminder email with prep instructions relevant to that service, a clear reschedule link, and a preferred send time. Patients who opt for fewer messages receive only essential reminders. Preference updates made in the portal flow back to the CDP and change future sends.
useCases.exampleBefore: All patients receive the same generic reminder email, sent at 8 a.m. on the day before the visit, with no prep details and a single unsubscribe option for all messages.
useCases.exampleAfter: A patient booked for a physical therapy session gets a reminder with warm-up instructions, a reschedule link, and a text-or-email choice, sent at their preferred time. Patients who limit messages receive only essential reminders, and unsubscribe rates fall.
toolsNeeded: Practice management or EHR scheduling system

source.title: personalized marketing campaigns: Healthcare Articles | MarketScale

useCases.title: Personalized Preventive Care Reminder Emails for Patients
useCases.oneLiner: Send patients screening and appointment reminders tailored to age, history, and declared preferences.
useCases.personalizationTactic: Tailor screening reminders by age, history, and channel preference
cdpDataUsed: Patient profile (first name, age, sex, location)
Declared communication preferences and topic interests
useCases.journey: A patient joins the provider's email list and declares preferred topics and contact frequency in a preference center. The CDP unifies profile, appointment, and care-gap data. When a screening or follow-up becomes due, the CDP triggers a reminder email whose content, timing, and call-to-action match the patient's age, sex, due item, and preferred frequency. If a patient opens but does not book, a single follow-up is sent after a set delay. Patients who stop engaging move to a lower-frequency educational track instead of being unsubscribed. Booking events and unsubscribes flow back to the CDP to suppress and refine future sends.
useCases.exampleBefore: A generic monthly newsletter goes to the entire patient list with the same "Schedule your checkup" message, regardless of age or care status.
useCases.exampleAfter: A 52-year-old patient overdue for a colorectal screening receives a short email with her name, the screening details, and a one-click booking link, sent on her preferred weekday morning. Patients who ignore it get one follow-up, then a lower-frequency track.

kpis.primary: Screening or appointment booking rate from reminder emails
secondary: Share of due screenings completed within 90 days

toolsNeeded: Email service provider with dynamic content

source.title: Personalized Email Marketing: A Healthcare Marketer's Guide

useCases.title: Propensity-Gated Retail Media and Onsite Personalization
useCases.oneLiner: Show sponsored offers only when a CDP propensity score says they match the shopper's needs.
useCases.personalizationTactic: Promote sponsored products only when propensity and relevance thresholds are met
cdpDataUsed: Declared preferences and zero-party survey answers
useCases.journey: A shopper browses the retailer's website or app. The CDP joins real-time session behavior with purchase history, loyalty activity, and predicted propensity scores to assign the shopper to a segment. Before any sponsored product appears in onsite placements, email, or app modules, a decision rule checks whether the product is relevant to the shopper's inferred need and whether the shopper's propensity to buy it clears a set threshold. If it fails, the shopper sees an organic, need-based recommendation instead. Results are reviewed in a test-and-learn loop that tracks both conversion and satisfaction, and the thresholds are adjusted over time.
useCases.exampleBefore: A shopper who bought a cordless drill sees a broad sponsored banner for unrelated paint brands on every page, and an email promotes a sponsored product from a category they have never browsed.
useCases.exampleAfter: The same shopper sees a relevant organic bundle of drill bits and a sponsored battery pack only because propensity and relevance scores clear the threshold, and unrelated sponsored placements are suppressed.

kpis.primary: Revenue per session from sponsored and organic recommendations combined

toolsNeeded: Customer Data Platform with identity resolution
Predictive modeling or ML platform for propensity scores

source.title: Unlocking Customer Growth: Driving High Value Actions Through Personalization and Retail Media | Deloitte US

useCases.title: Behavioral Persona Website and Email Personalization
useCases.oneLiner: Classify shoppers into live behavioral personas to tailor site experiences and triggered emails.
useCases.personalizationTactic: Behavior-based personas drive on-site content and triggered emails
cdpDataUsed: Granular web behavioral events (clicks, searches, filters, sort order)
Persistent customer ID stitched across sessions
useCases.journey: A shopper arrives on the site from paid search or a mobile device. The CDP checks their behavioral persona based on recent events, such as frequent sales-page visits or price-based sorting (value hunter), repeated basket abandonment (frequent abandoner), or interest in new arrivals (on-trend). The site then shows matching content, such as price-led banners, a bag-completion incentive, or the latest product edits. If the shopper leaves with items in the bag or after browsing without buying, the CDP triggers a matching email (browse-not-bought, abandoned basket, or new-arrivals aspiration) and suppresses the email if the shopper has already purchased.
useCases.exampleBefore: All visitors see the same homepage and sale banners. Abandoned-basket emails go to everyone at the same time with a generic discount.
useCases.exampleAfter: A price-sorting visitor sees value-focused product rails and a price-drop email. A frequent abandoner sees a bag-completion offer on return, and an on-trend shopper gets new-arrival emails.

useCases.title: Abandoned cart recovery with dynamic product recommendations
useCases.oneLiner: Triggered cart reminders that show live stock, price, and recommended items for each shopper.
useCases.personalizationTactic: Cart reminders with live stock and tailored recommendations
useCases.journey: A shopper adds items to cart on the website or app and leaves without checking out. The CDP detects the abandonment event and waits a short window, then checks live inventory and price for the cart items. If the items are still available, the shopper receives an email or app push with the cart items, any price or stock change, and two to four recommended products based on past purchases and browsing. If a cart item is out of stock, the message suggests similar in-stock alternatives instead. Loyalty members see their tier perk applied to the cart. Messages stop once the shopper purchases or the cart is emptied.
useCases.exampleBefore: Generic email: "You left items in your cart. Complete your order now." Same message for every shopper, with an out-of-stock item listed as available.
useCases.exampleAfter: Push: "Your linen throw is back in stock in Sand. Gold members get 10% off today. Customers who bought this also liked the matching cushions." Only in-stock items are shown and the offer matches the shopper's tier.

secondary: Discount cost as % of recovered revenue

toolsNeeded: CDP with web and app SDK

source.title: Personalization in Retail Guide With Examples | Braze

useCases.title: Dynamic service-icon ordering for first-time telecom homepage visitors
useCases.oneLiner: A telecom operator used dynamic icon allocation to surface ecosystem services for unknown homepage visitors.
useCases.personalizationTactic: Dynamic service icon ordering for unknown homepage visitors
cdpDataUsed: Real-time on-site interaction and widget CTR for homepage visitors
Visitor status (new vs. returning) used to split results
useCases.journey: Unauthenticated visitors arriving from organic search land on the homepage, where the operator's ecosystem services are shown as icons. Because the company had no data on these visitors, a machine-learning engine dynamically ordered the service icons per visitor in real time, compared against a control group with a fixed icon order.
